output.query: timing of anticoagulation initiation after acute cardioembolic ischemic stroke atrial fibrillation

results.authors: Powers WJ, Rabinstein AA, et al.
results.key_finding: For patients with AF-related ischemic stroke, initiation of oral anticoagulation between 4 and 14 days after stroke onset is reasonable depending on infarct size and hemorrhagic transformation risk.
results.title: 2019 AHA/ASA Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke

results.key_finding: Early initiation of DOACs (within 48h for minor stroke, within 6-7 days for moderate stroke) was non-inferior to later initiation in preventing recurrent stroke or systemic embolism.
results.title: ELAN Trial: Early versus Late Anticoagulation in Stroke with AF

results.key_finding: Apixaban is preferred in patients with CKD stage 3-4 due to lower renal clearance (25%) compared to rivaroxaban (33%) or dabigatran (80%).
results.title: DOAC Selection in CKD: Apixaban vs Rivaroxaban

output.summary: Current evidence supports initiating oral anticoagulation with a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) within 4-14 days after cardioembolic ischemic stroke, with timing guided by infarct size and hemorrhagic transformation risk. The ELAN trial demonstrated that earlier initiation was non-inferior to delayed initiation. In patients with chronic kidney disease, DOACs with lower renal clearance (e.g., apixaban, approximately 25% renal elimination) may be preferred over those with higher renal dependence. DOACs are generally preferred over warfarin for non-valvular atrial fibrillation given their favorable safety and efficacy profiles.

alternatives: Mechanical thrombectomy for a confirmed large-vessel occlusion, especially if thrombolysis is contraindicated by an elevated INR.
Resume/again establish oral anticoagulation (DOAC or warfarin) for AF-related cardioembolism once hemorrhagic-transformation risk is acceptable; counsel on adherence given prior self-discontinuation.
contraindications: IV alteplase is contraindicated if INR >1.7 or PT abnormally elevated. Given warfarin was stopped about 3 weeks ago, the INR has most likely normalized, but it MUST be confirmed before thrombolysis.

key_clinical_evidence: Acute ischemic stroke is a clinical syndrome plus neuroimaging diagnosis; CT first excludes hemorrhage and unmasks the tPA decision
Time of last known well governs IV thrombolysis eligibility (≤4.5h standard; selected up to 9h with imaging mismatch per WAKE-UP/EXTEND)
proximal vascular occlusion on CTA opens the mechanical thrombectomy pathway up to 24h per DAWN/DEFUSE-3 selection criteria
TOAST classification by mechanism (large-artery, cardioembolic, small-vessel, other, undetermined) drives secondary prevention strategy
Normal sinus rhythm on initial ECG does NOT exclude paroxysmal AF — extended cardiac monitoring is required, especially in cryptogenic stroke
AF + HFrEF doubles cardioembolic stroke risk; both warrant anticoagulation
Concurrent LV thrombus on echo would dictate at least 3 months of anticoagulation independent of AF
DOAC dose adjustment for CKD is essential
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=amyloid_PET): Amyloid PET has no role in acute ischemic stroke evaluation and incurs substantial cost without altering management
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=DaTscan): Dopamine transporter SPECT is indicated for parkinsonian syndromes, not vascular stroke workup
Off-pathway modality for order_advanced_imaging (modality=FDG_PET): FDG-PET (neurodegenerative/oncologic indications) has no role in routine ischemic stroke workup
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: Non-contrast CT is the required first-line study in the acute window; MRI adds tissue-based selection and is not mandatory for the diagnosis.

AHA/ASA 2026 sequencing: glucose is checked before thrombolysis, but routine CBC/coagulation results are not awaited without a reason to expect abnormality; ECG/troponin do not delay reperfusion, and CTA/CTP do not wait for creatinine.

case_body_concerns: Gaze-direction inconsistency: cranial_nerves describes 'Conjugate right gaze deviation' but this is a LEFT MCA stroke with right-sided hemiparesis. Cortical (destructive) gaze deviation is toward the lesion, i.e. eyes should deviate LEFT (away from the weak right side). 'Right gaze deviation' is the wrong direction for a left-hemisphere lesion. Flagged for clinician adjudication (would likely correct to 'left gaze deviation/preference').

Minor HPI wording slip: 'The daughter reports that he spoke to his mother on the phone at approximately 09:00' — likely intended that the daughter spoke to the patient; the patient (age 55) speaking to his mother is implausible and reads as a template copy artifact.
clinical_pearls: Self-discontinuation of anticoagulation is a common real-world scenario leading to cardioembolic stroke; always inquire about medication adherence
In patients with CKD, apixaban is the preferred DOAC due to its lower dependence on renal clearance (25% renal elimination)
Spontaneous echo contrast ('smoke') in the left atrium on echocardiography indicates blood stasis and markedly elevated thromboembolic risk
The ELAN trial supports earlier initiation of DOACs (within 6-7 days for moderate strokes) compared to traditional 14-day waiting periods

patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Pradeep Singh is a 55-year-old right-handed South Asian man with a history of atrial fibrillation (previously on warfarin, self-discontinued 3 weeks ago), hypertension, type 2 diabetes, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, and chronic kidney disease who was brought to the emergency department by his daughter after the acute onset of right-sided weakness and speech difficulties. The daughter reports that he spoke to his mother on the phone at approximately 09:00 this morning and he sounded completely normal, discussing plans for a church event this weekend. The daughter stopped by to drop off groceries at 10:45 and found him sitting on the kitchen floor, leaning against the refrigerator, with his right arm limp and speech garbled. The patient was able to say 'help' and 'arm' but could not form complete sentences. He appeared to have been attempting to reach the phone. There was a broken coffee mug on the floor beside him. The daughter immediately called 911. EMS arrived at 11:02 and documented right facial droop, right upper and lower extremity weakness, and expressive aphasia. A prehospital stroke alert was activated. Field glucose was 142 mg/dL. The patient was transported to our comprehensive stroke center, arriving at 11:28. On the cardiac monitor he was found to be in atrial fibrillation with a rate of 108 bpm. He was mildly hypertensive at 192/104 mmHg. He was anxious, tearful, and attempting to speak but producing only fragments and paraphasic errors. When asked why he stopped his warfarin, his daughter explained that he had noticed large bruises on his arms and legs over the past month and decided on his own to stop the medication without consulting his physician. There is no history of recent head trauma, seizure, fever, or new headache. His last known well time is established at 09:00, approximately 2 hours and 28 minutes before ED arrival.
